1803bc0983463103.text:
{"criticisms": [
 {"element": "Contact multiplier",
  "quote": "STEP(1, Measures_start) - STEP(1, Measures_start + Measures_length)",
  "kind": "information",
  "why": "The measures switch on and off on calendar dates fixed in advance. The authority sees admissions and beds occupied every day, but the rule reads neither, so the model cannot represent an authority that acts on what it sees. That is fine for comparing dated policies; it is not a decision rule.",
  "suggestion": "Add a rule that starts and stops the measures from Beds occupied, perhaps through a reporting delay, and compare it with the dated policies."},
 {"element": "Admissions",
  "quote": "Hospital_share * Infectious / Infectious_period",
  "kind": "constant",
  "why": "Hospital share is a single constant with no stated source. Early admissions identify only the share times the number infected, so a wrong share scales the whole bed forecast up or down.",
  "suggestion": "State where the share comes from and carry a range through the forecast."},
 {"element": "Incubating",
  "quote": "Exposed_1 / (Latent_period / 2)",
  "kind": "constant",
  "why": "The 2 is the number of latent stages, written by hand into Incubating and again into Becoming infectious. If someone changes one and not the other, the mean latent period changes without warning.",
  "suggestion": "Name it Latent stages and use the name in both flows."},
 {"element": "Bed capacity",
  "quote": "Surge_beds * MIN(1, RAMP(1 / Surge_build_time, Surge_start))",
  "kind": "units",
  "why": "RAMP rises at 1 / Surge_build_time per day, so after t days it is a pure number, and MIN caps it at 1. Surge beds times a fraction is beds, so the units balance.",
  "suggestion": "None: the rule is sound."},
 {"element": "Effective R",
  "quote": "R0 * Contact_multiplier * Susceptible / Population",
  "kind": "information",
  "why": "Effective R reads the true susceptible share, which the authority cannot see. That is acceptable for an output, but not for an input to any decision rule.",
  "suggestion": "Keep it as an output; make sure no policy rule reads it."},
 {"element": "Bed capacity",
  "quote": "Base_beds * Occupancy_target",
  "kind": "constant",
  "why": "Hospitals plan to an occupancy of about 85%, so the usable capacity is lower than Base beds, and the 0.85 has no stated source.",
  "suggestion": "Name the occupancy target and give its source."},
 {"element": "Patients without a bed",
  "quote": "MAX(0, Beds_occupied - Bed_capacity)",
  "kind": "other",
  "why": "Patients above capacity keep the same stay and the same discharge as everyone else, and none die. When beds run out, outcomes would change, so this measures pressure on the hospital, not harm to patients.",
  "suggestion": "Say so in the brief, or add worse outcomes for patients without a bed."}
]}

87997c74e360fc48.text: Without action, the epidemic would overwhelm the region's 1,000 beds, with occupancy peaking at about 4,800 and about 108,000 patient-days without a bed. Surge beds alone, or a lasting 30% cut in contacts alone, would each roughly halve that shortage. Together, they will cut patient-days without a bed by 94%, to about 6,700, and shorten the time over capacity from about 53 days to 26. Across nine plausible versions of the epidemic, the combined plan does best on average (about 17,300 patient-days without a bed) and in the worst case (70,700, against at least 122,600 for any other plan). These are model results, and the forecast will sharpen as more admissions are seen.
